plan.contextChunk: This figure is a plain black-and-white line drawing of a trough in oblique three-dimensional view, with no shading or color. The body is a long open channel whose cross section is a parabola: the near end at the left is drawn as a U-shaped curve narrowing to a rounded point at the bottom, the same curve repeats at the far end on the right, and straight lines join the two rims along the length so the opening runs uniformly from end to end. Three measurements are marked. A double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end spans from the top rim down to the lowest point of the curve, labeled 18 in. A label along the upper front edge reads 3 ft for the length. A short segment across the far end of the top rim reads 12 in for the width across the opening. The flat rectangle formed by the rims and connecting lines represents the open water surface. Giving depth, length, and top width against a visible parabolic profile supplies just the quantities needed to fit an equation to the cross section and then write the water's surface area as a function of its depth.

elements: near-end parabolic cross-section outline (U-shaped curve, open at top, rounded vertex at bottom)
far-end parabolic cross-section outline (identical curve, offset along the receding length direction)
front rim line joining the two parabola left/front lips
back rim line joining the two parabola right/back lips
flat rectangular top opening (the open water-surface plane) bounded by the two rims and the two end chords
ruled parabolic channel surface (lofted between the two end curves) forming the trough wall
double-headed vertical dimension arrow inside the near end from top rim to vertex, labeled '18 in'
length label '3 ft' along the upper front edge
short top-rim segment with tick marks at the far end labeled '12 in'
water body: horizontal plane inside the trough at the current depth, plus its shaded volume down to the parabolic wall
water-surface rectangle highlighted on top of the water body (width x length)
2D cross-section panel: x-y axes in inches, fitted parabola y = 0.5x^2, rim points (-6,18) and (6,18), horizontal water line at current depth with endpoints and width bracket
readout of surface half-width, full width, and surface area

interactions.teaches: how the physical 18 in depth and 12 in top width of the trough pin down the parabola y = 0.5x^2 that describes the end profile
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: the width of the water surface is a function of depth, not a constant — it shrinks toward zero at the vertex and reaches 12 in only at the rim
interactions.label: Water depth (in)

interactions.teaches: surface area is the depth-dependent width multiplied by the length; stretching the trough changes area linearly while the cross section is unchanged
interactions.label: Trough length (ft)

interactions.teaches: the water width is derived from whatever curve bounds the cross section — change the profile and the same depth gives a different surface width and area
interactions.label: End profile (inches, vertex at origin)

demo_steps.title: The trough as drawn
demo_steps.narration: A 3 ft open channel whose cross section is a parabola 18 in deep and 12 in across the top; the rims and connecting lines bound the open surface.

demo_steps.title: Fit the parabola
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the end view: putting the vertex at the origin, the rim points (-6, 18) and (6, 18) force y = 0.5x^2 as the cross-section equation.

demo_steps.title: Lower the water
demo_steps.narration: Drop the water line to 8 in. Solving 8 = 0.5x^2 gives x = 4, so the surface is only 8 in wide — width depends on depth.

demo_steps.title: Surface area in 3D
demo_steps.narration: Back in the channel, that 8 in wide strip runs the full 3 ft length: area = 2*sqrt(2d) * L.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the channel
demo_steps.narration: Lengthening the trough to 5 ft leaves the cross section untouched but scales the water-surface rectangle, and with it the area.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Work in inches, then scale to world units with 1 world unit = 6 in (default trough: X width 2, Y depth 3, Z length 6). Oblique pose: the true, undistorted face is the NEAR end parabola drawn in the X-Y plane at the LEFT of the frame (+X screen-right = 12 in top width, +Y screen-up = 18 in depth, vertex at origin pointing down); the length recedes along +Z toward the UPPER-RIGHT diagonal exactly as in the source, so the far-end parabola sits up and right of the near one. Cross-section curve: y = (18/6^2)x^2 = 0.5 x^2 for x in [-6, 6] inches, vertex (0,0), rim points (-6,18) and (6,18). Water surface half-width at depth d: x = sqrt(d/0.5) = sqrt(2d); full width w(d) = 2*sqrt(2d) in (w(18)=12 in); surface area A = w(d) * L, with L in inches (3 ft = 36 in). Length slider 1-6 ft maps to Z span 2-12 world units; width and depth never change with the length slider. Labels as in the source: '18 in' on a vertical double-headed arrow inside the near-end curve from rim (0,18) to vertex (0,0); '3 ft' centered above the front rim line running along the receding diagonal; '12 in' on a short ticked segment across the FAR end top rim at upper right. Palette: pure line-art on white background — outlines #1a1a1a at ~2 px, labels black sans-serif; add-ons only: water fill translucent blue #4da6ff at 0.35 alpha with a solid #1f6fb2 surface edge, water-surface rectangle highlighted #2b8cbe, dimension arrows #333, cross-section axes light grey #888 with the parabola in #1a1a1a.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the trough wall as a lofted/parametric BufferGeometry: sample the profile y(x) at ~64 x-samples, extrude along Z into a ribbon mesh with DoubleSide MeshBasicMaterial (flat white) plus a separate LineSegments overlay for the two end curves and the two rim lines so it reads as line art. Use an OrthographicCamera with a fixed oblique (cabinet-style) shear — depth axis at ~30 deg screen angle, foreshortened to ~0.5 — rather than a perspective camera; no orbit. Water volume: same lofted surface clipped above y=d, capped by a horizontal plane at y=d spanning x in [-sqrt(2d), sqrt(2d)]; rebuild geometry on slider change (cheap at this vertex count). Cross-section view is the same scene with the camera swung to a straight front-on orthographic view plus a 2D axis/label overlay drawn in CSS or with Line2 — animate the transition over ~0.6 s so the learner sees the end face rotate flat. Equation input: parse with a small safe evaluator (mathjs-style), clamp to the domain [-6,6], find the water half-width by bisection on y(x)=d instead of assuming the closed form, and surface inline 'could not parse' / 'not increasing from the vertex' errors without resetting the scene. Text labels via CSS2DRenderer so '18 in', '3 ft', '12 in' stay crisp and screen-aligned.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for water depth: the learner raises and lowers a horizontal fill line inside the parabolic cross section and the water surface width changes, making clear that width is a function of depth rather than a constant.
- Toggle between 3D trough and cross-section graph: the learner switches from the channel view to the fitted parabola using 18 in depth and 12 in top width, making clear how the physical dimensions determine the equation for the end profile.
- Slider for trough length: the learner adjusts the 3 ft length and the water surface rectangle extends while the cross-section stays fixed, making clear how cross-sectional width and length combine to determine surface area.
- Equation input for the trough cross-section: learner edits a parabolic profile or the 18 in depth and 12 in width constraints; the cross-section and 3D trough fill redraw so width is derived from the entered curve.

authoredContext:
For example, suppose the Sustainability Club builds a water runoff collector in the shape of a parabolic trough as shown in the figure. We can use the information in the figure to find the surface area of the water in the trough as a function of the depth of the water.

Diagram of a parabolic trough that is 18” in height, 3’ in length, and 12” in width.

Because it will be helpful to have an equation for the parabolic cross-sectional shape, we will impose a coordinate system at the cross section, with x measured horizontally and y measured vertically, with the origin at the vertex of the parabola. See the figure.

discrepancies: Default state shows a half-full blue water body plus a highlighted surface rectangle; the source trough is empty, so at a glance the figure reads as a water-level problem rather than the plain dimensioned trough (set default depth to 0 or make water opt-in).
The 'surface 8.49 in × 36 in' cyan annotation sits on top of the trough wall/water boundary and clutters the interior where the source has only the clean 18-in dimension arrow.
The '18 in' text is placed just left of the dimension line and collides with the near-end rim chord, whereas in the source it sits cleanly inside the parabola beside the arrow.

Projection/opening: the top rim quad is drawn wide and viewed from noticeably higher than the source, so the open channel looks like a shallow wedge from above rather than the narrow deep parabolic gutter seen almost edge-on in the original.

The far-end bottom of the source shows the closed parabolic end sweeping up toward the far top corner; in the generated view the far end reads as an open flat cut, weakening the 'gutter with an end' impression.
evaluation.notes: Faithful lofted parabolic trough with correct 3 ft / 12 in / 18 in dimensions and an excellent set of pedagogically meaningful controls (depth, length, editable profile, 2D cross-section toggle, guided steps); main weaknesses are the non-source water fill shown by default and some crowded interior annotations, plus a slightly high/wide viewpoint compared with the original.
action_items: Initialize water depth at 0 (or add an explicit 'show water' toggle) so the default view matches the empty dimensioned trough of the source.
Move the 'surface w × L' label outside the trough (e.g. above the far rim) and nudge the '18 in' label clear of the near-end chord line.
Lower the default camera elevation / reduce the depth shear slightly so the parabolic end reads as a deep narrow gutter as in the source rather than a wide open wedge.
Emphasize the far-end profile curve (and its tick marks) so the closed far end and the '12 in' measurement read as clearly as in the original.
plan_action_items: Plan the water-level exploration as a secondary state layered onto a faithful empty-trough default, rather than the initial appearance of the figure.

feedback.rationale: The concept and control set are correct; the issues are concrete implementation fixes (default water depth 0, label placement, camera elevation, far-end profile emphasis) rather than a flawed interaction plan.

demo_steps.title: The trough as drawn
demo_steps.narration: A 3 ft open channel whose cross section is a parabola 18 in deep and 12 in across the top; the rims and connecting lines bound the open surface.

demo_steps.title: Fit the parabola
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the end view: putting the vertex at the origin, the rim points (-6, 18) and (6, 18) force y = 0.5x^2 as the cross-section equation.

demo_steps.title: Lower the water
demo_steps.narration: Drop the water line to 8 in. Solving 8 = 0.5x^2 gives x = 4, so the surface is only 8 in wide — width depends on depth.

demo_steps.title: Surface area in 3D
demo_steps.narration: Back in the channel, that 8 in wide strip runs the full 3 ft length: area = 2*sqrt(2d) * L.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the channel
demo_steps.narration: Lengthening the trough to 5 ft leaves the cross section untouched but scales the water-surface rectangle, and with it the area.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Work in inches, then scale to world units with 1 world unit = 6 in (default trough: X width 2, Y depth 3, Z length 6). Oblique pose: the true, undistorted face is the NEAR end parabola drawn in the X-Y plane at the LEFT of the frame (+X screen-right = 12 in top width, +Y screen-up = 18 in depth, vertex at origin pointing down); the length recedes along +Z toward the UPPER-RIGHT diagonal exactly as in the source, so the far-end parabola sits up and right of the near one. Cross-section curve: y = (18/6^2)x^2 = 0.5 x^2 for x in [-6, 6] inches, vertex (0,0), rim points (-6,18) and (6,18). Water surface half-width at depth d: x = sqrt(d/0.5) = sqrt(2d); full width w(d) = 2*sqrt(2d) in (w(18)=12 in); surface area A = w(d) * L, with L in inches (3 ft = 36 in). Length slider 1-6 ft maps to Z span 2-12 world units; width and depth never change with the length slider. Labels as in the source: '18 in' on a vertical double-headed arrow inside the near-end curve from rim (0,18) to vertex (0,0); '3 ft' centered above the front rim line running along the receding diagonal; '12 in' on a short ticked segment across the FAR end top rim at upper right. Palette: pure line-art on white background — outlines #1a1a1a at ~2 px, labels black sans-serif; add-ons only: water fill translucent blue #4da6ff at 0.35 alpha with a solid #1f6fb2 surface edge, water-surface rectangle highlighted #2b8cbe, dimension arrows #333, cross-section axes light grey #888 with the parabola in #1a1a1a.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the trough wall as a lofted/parametric BufferGeometry: sample the profile y(x) at ~64 x-samples, extrude along Z into a ribbon mesh with DoubleSide MeshBasicMaterial (flat white) plus a separate LineSegments overlay for the two end curves and the two rim lines so it reads as line art. Use an OrthographicCamera with a fixed oblique (cabinet-style) shear — depth axis at ~30 deg screen angle, foreshortened to ~0.5 — rather than a perspective camera; no orbit. Water volume: same lofted surface clipped above y=d, capped by a horizontal plane at y=d spanning x in [-sqrt(2d), sqrt(2d)]; rebuild geometry on slider change (cheap at this vertex count). Cross-section view is the same scene with the camera swung to a straight front-on orthographic view plus a 2D axis/label overlay drawn in CSS or with Line2 — animate the transition over ~0.6 s so the learner sees the end face rotate flat. Equation input: parse with a small safe evaluator (mathjs-style), clamp to the domain [-6,6], find the water half-width by bisection on y(x)=d instead of assuming the closed form, and surface inline 'could not parse' / 'not increasing from the vertex' errors without resetting the scene. Text labels via CSS2DRenderer so '18 in', '3 ft', '12 in' stay crisp and screen-aligned.
